mappings.note: The 36-outcome sample space for two distinguishable dice must be sized (LO-1), then 'sum is 8' broken into the five ordered pairs and counted (LO-3). The (2,6)/(6,2) distinction is why both steps carry marks.

A proof that P(E)+P(not E)=1, i.e. that the scale tops out at certainty (C-6.2-LO-1), argued by partitioning n outcomes into m and n-m (C-9.1-LO-3). Not LO-2 or LO-3 of C-6.2: nothing experimental is involved.
The defining formula for experimental probability, trials-with-the-outcome over total trials. C-6.2-LO-2's 'obtained by repeating a trial'.
Why the two values differ is the LO-2 distinction; the closing point that the gap narrows as trials grow is LO-3. The item needs both, which is why it is not cited to either alone.

The trap is treating an EXPERIMENTAL zero as proof of impossibility, which confuses the two kinds of probability (LO-2); the reason statement, that 0 denotes impossibility, is the true endpoint fact (C-6.2-LO-1).
Computes 108/200 from observed trials. That is experimental probability, LO-2; LO-3 is not cited because the value is never compared with the theoretical one.
Explicitly sets the experimental 0.2 beside the theoretical one sixth (LO-2) and then judges whether 120 trials make the gap meaningful, which is the law-of-large-numbers reasoning of LO-3.
Two relative frequencies from 500 tosses, with the check that they sum to 1. Experimental probability only -- no theoretical comparison, so not LO-3.
The running-relative-frequency graph settling onto the 0.5 line as trials increase IS the law of large numbers pictured. LO-3; LO-2 would stop at computing one relative frequency.
Five heads running, then the next toss: the gambler's-fallacy item in its purest form, LO-4.
'A head is due' explained away by independence and by the coin having no memory. LO-4's 'explains why earlier results do not alter the probability of the next trial'.
A false assertion (a tail is more likely after three heads) against a true reason (tosses are independent) -- the assertion-reason form of the gambler's fallacy, LO-4.

Independence is the concept, tested from the other side: drawing WITHOUT replacement makes trials dependent. LO-4 owns independence in this frame, even though its wording is about a fair repeated experiment.
Where the experimental value tends as trials increase -- LO-3's statement of the law of large numbers, in one line.
The law of large numbers stated, plus the crucial caveat that it promises proportions and not equal counts. LO-3; the caveat is what keeps it from being an LO-4 item.
The classic false assertion that the NUMBERS of heads and tails become equal, set against the true statement about relative frequency. That counts-versus-proportion distinction is the heart of LO-3.
Designs the demonstration -- what to record, how to plot it and what to expect. LO-3 as a practical task rather than a statement.
What 'biased' means for a die, i.e. that its faces are not equally likely. LO-5 is the fairness outcome; LO-3 is about convergence, which is not in question here.
Judges fairness FROM the outcomes produced -- 30 sixes in 60 -- and notes that no finite experiment settles it with certainty. LO-5 exactly, with an LO-3 flavour in the caveat.
Designs a fairness investigation and states what makes the conclusion trustworthy. LO-5's judging clause; qid:706835 is the LO-3 twin of this item, which is why the two get different codes.

The answer names the gambler's fallacy first (LO-4) and then over-reading a small sample (LO-3's convergence caveat). Cited to those two rather than LO-5, since no specific coin or die is being judged.
What probability measures, answered directly as a scale from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain. C-6.2-LO-1's definition.
Four of the five terms defined -- experiment, outcome, sample space, event -- are the vocabulary of C-9.1-LO-1; the fifth, probability itself, is defined on the 0-1 scale (C-6.2-LO-1).

Randomness is defined by the two halves the answer gives: the outcomes CAN all be listed in advance (C-9.1-LO-1's sample space) while the individual result cannot be predicted and only the long-run pattern is (C-6.2-LO-3). No single outcome in this frame defines a random experiment.

False precisely because the sample space CAN be listed in advance -- the statement LO-1 rests on. Cited alone here, unlike qid:706842, because unpredictability of the individual trial is not at issue.
A tree is asked for by name, with the two stages and the four paths read off it. C-9.1-LO-2, not LO-1: the method is the point, since the sample space could also be listed directly.
A two-stage tree over UNLIKE experiments, coin then die, giving twelve paths. LO-2's 'experiment carried out in stages ... reads the outcomes of the combined experiment from its branches'.
Three stages and eight endpoints drawn as a tree (LO-2), and then 'exactly two heads' decomposed into HHT, HTH and THH and counted (LO-3). The second step is what distinguishes it from qid:706844.
